text: The whiteboard design becomes real tables now. Riverside_DW, a brand-new warehouse database, gets three dimension tables: dim_date, dim_store, and dim_product — the clean, conformed side of the pipeline the transform step will look values up against.

dim_date is never loaded by the nightly process at all — it's static reference data, bulk-populated years ahead with a single set-based script, so nothing downstream ever has to calculate a date part at query time.
dim_store gets seeded once with Riverside's known fourteen stores — small, simple, done.

dim_product is where the Type 2 structure from the whiteboard becomes real columns — is_current, effective_date, expiration_date — with a covering index on SKU and is_current, because that's the exact lookup pattern the SSIS transform will hit on every single row, every single night. Building it right now means not discovering it's slow three videos from now.
The initial catalog loads as a one-time import, every row's is_current set to one. Future price changes get handled by real SSIS logic later, never by editing this table by hand.
Before moving to the fact table, one sanity check: exactly one current row per SKU, zero duplicates. With all three dimensions standing, the center of the star is next.
